newsitem.title: USA: Music community honors bluesman John Lee Hooker.
newsitem.headline: Music community honors bluesman John Lee Hooker.

text.p: John Lee Hooker was the toast of the town on Thursday night as the U.S. music industry honoured the blues legend at a star-studded ceremony.

Guests such as Bonnie Raitt, Ruth Brown and Robert Cray looked on as B.B. King presented his longtime friend with the Blues Foundation's second annual lifetime achievement award at King's own nightclub in Universal City.

Along with King, Hooker is the last of the great blues musicians from the Mississippi Delta, a region whose native sons such as Robert Johnson and Muddy Waters helped pave the way for rock and roll music in the late 1940s.

Hooker, with his blues-based boogie, is best known for such songs as "Boogie Chillen" and "Boom Boom." He won a Grammy this year for his most recent album, "Chill Out," and his next album is due out early next year.
"So good," mumbled Hooker, 76, dressed in black suit, shirt, fedora and dark glasses with a red shirt, as he accepted his award.
Staring menacingly at a television camera, he asked, "Am I gonna be on TV?" As the laughter subsided, he muttered "Goodbye" and staggered off-stage.

More effusive was Hooker's frequent collaborator Raitt, who earlier told the audience, "I don't know what it is to this day that makes that black snake moan -- but with 18 grandchildren, I think he may know something about it."

Raitt said her life was forever changed when she first heard a Hooker album at the age of 14. She took to listening to other artists such as Howlin' Wolf, Muddy Waters and the Rolling Stones while her mother begged her to go back to the more clean-cut Beatles. "I just never went back," Raitt said.

Injecting some solemnity to the occasion, she paid tribute to Hooker's business acumen, noting that too many blues singers have died prematurely because of the shabby way they were treated by the music industry.
King said, "Nobody can sing the blues or play them the style that John does. And even when you try and try hard, you don't sound good. It's only John Lee Hooker that's so good at it."
The Blues Foundation is a non-profit organisation that preserves and promotes the blues.
